item.text: {"facts":[{"source_id":"SRC-2f5d175050c09c8f","start_unit":5,"end_unit":5,"fact_summary":"In March 2023, the GIEI reported that the Mexican authorities, COVAJ and UEILCA agreed to activate existing arrest warrants, pursue investigations into authorship, obstruction and torture, provide GIEI access to prisons and proceedings, and provide targeted information from Sedena and Semar; the GIEI mandate was extended to June 2023.","question_ids":["3B.4","3B.10","4B.4","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"favorable","period_fit":"The report was issued on 31 March 2023 and describes actions and commitments during AMLO's administration.","ruler_attribution":"The report describes commitments by Mexican authorities and records that the president ordered access to relevant archives; it does not attribute every institutional action personally to López Obrador.","limitations":["The source records agreements and intended actions, not complete implementation or outcomes."]},{"source_id":"SRC-2f5d175050c09c8f","start_unit":9,"end_unit":13,"fact_summary":"The GIEI reported evidence that military and intelligence authorities had real-time information about the Ayotzinapa attacks and disappearances, concealed or denied relevant records, changed or contradicted accounts, and failed to protect or rescue the students; it also reported that Sedena denied documents later found in its archives and that some arrest warrants remained inactive.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.9","3B.10","4B.4","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.9","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The 2023 report evaluates the handling of a 2014 case and continuing investigation during AMLO's presidency.","ruler_attribution":"The findings concern Sedena, CISEN and other authorities; they show institutional noncompliance with presidential information requests but do not establish that López Obrador personally ordered concealment.","limitations":["Several findings concern events before 2018, while the report assesses their investigation and disclosure during the target period.","The report distinguishes documented evidence from allegations and unresolved issues."]},{"source_id":"SRC-2f5d175050c09c8f","start_unit":17,"end_unit":24,"fact_summary":"The GIEI reported that Marina had concealed secret operations and torture, that the prior official account was contradicted by forensic evidence, and that investigations were obstructed by falsified records, torture-tainted statements, withheld military files, withdrawn arrest warrants, pressure on the special prosecutor, staff turnover and continuing delays; it also credited advances by Fiscal Omar Gómez's team and noted some later cooperation by Marina.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.9","3B.10","4B.4","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.10","8B.5","8B.6","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The report was issued in 2023 and covers both inherited abuses and the administration's continuing investigative response.","ruler_attribution":"The source attributes conduct to multiple agencies and prosecutors; it records presidential authorization for archive access and public commitments but does not prove personal direction of each obstruction or correction.","limitations":["The report is an expert investigative synthesis rather than a final judicial determination for every allegation.","It reports both progress and unresolved institutional failures."]},{"source_id":"SRC-75fde37e1388716b","start_unit":6,"end_unit":13,"fact_summary":"The Human Rights Committee follow-up records Mexican measures including a bill to regulate temporary military participation in public security, military human-rights and humanitarian-law training, victim-reparation orders, a special prosecutor's expanded jurisdiction, an anonymous complaints channel, and judicial and investigatory reforms; it nevertheless records concerns about militarization, systemic impunity, insufficient protection for journalists and defenders, weak investigative capacity, and inadequate due-process safeguards.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.8","3B.10","4B.3","4B.4","4B.6","4B.9","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.6","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The document is dated 28 August 2023 but much of the underlying state information covers 2019-2021 and follow-up through 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The document attributes measures to the Mexican state and government, not exclusively to López Obrador.","limitations":["The extracted text is an HTML rendering with encoding corruption.","The Committee's observations include historical measures and requested future actions, limiting direct inference about 2023 implementation."]},{"source_id":"SRC-e3b2bc1e13c9c975","start_unit":1,"end_unit":12,"fact_summary":"Mexico presided over the Second Meeting of States Parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in November-December 2023; the meeting adopted a declaration reaffirming prohibition, complete elimination, evidence-based scientific advice, stakeholder participation, and rejection of nuclear threats, and appointed Mexico as gender focal point for implementation work.","question_ids":["1B.1","1B.2","1B.4","1B.7","1B.10","8B.2","8B.5","8B.6","8B.10"],"polarity":"favorable","period_fit":"The meeting occurred from 27 November to 1 December 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The document attributes the presidency and institutional roles to Mexico and its representatives; it does not establish personal decisions by López Obrador.","limitations":["The source concerns Mexico's multilateral role and treaty proceedings, not domestic nuclear-risk policy or direct presidential conduct.","The declaration is collective and does not demonstrate implementation beyond the meeting."]},{"source_id":"SRC-0bb2a7dfa4641777","start_unit":74,"end_unit":76,"fact_summary":"On 29 December 2023, López Obrador inaugurated a 40,000-square-meter centralized medicine warehouse intended to supply hospitals nationwide, with delivery by the armed forces or Birmex within 24-48 hours; AP reported severe prior shortages, including unfilled prescriptions rising from 1.5 million in 2019 to 22 million in 2021 and about 12.5 million in 2022, while experts questioned the system's logistics and centralization risks.","question_ids":["3B.6","3B.9","3B.10","5B.1","5B.6","5B.7","5B.9","5B.10","6B.1","6B.2","6B.4","6B.5","6B.6","6B.9","6B.10","8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The inauguration occurred at the end of 2023 and the article reports medication-access conditions and policy decisions during the preceding years.","ruler_attribution":"The article directly identifies the warehouse as López Obrador's solution and quotes his delivery pledge.","limitations":["The source reports the launch and historical shortages, not whether the warehouse achieved reliable nationwide delivery.","Several shortage figures are attributed to the civic group Zero Shortages and may reflect reporting and pandemic effects."]},{"source_id":"SRC-989a4ab71d7e1333","start_unit":6,"end_unit":15,"fact_summary":"CONEVAL reported that in 2023 it produced multidimensional poverty and social-rights indicators, coordinated 173 evaluations, published monitoring and evaluation products, analyzed health access and women's rights, and supplied evidence for budgetary and program improvements; it also reported 1,218 identified uses of its information in 2023, a 34.4% increase over the historical average.","question_ids":["5B.6","5B.7","5B.8","5B.10","6B.2","6B.3","6B.5","6B.8","6B.10","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"favorable","period_fit":"The report covers January-December 2023 results, with some contextual material extending into June 2024.","ruler_attribution":"CONEVAL is a constitutionally mandated institution operating within the national policy framework; the report does not show that López Obrador personally used each finding or adopted each recommendation.","limitations":["The reported uses measure identified use of information, not independently verified improvement in outcomes.","The report is self-reported institutional performance and does not establish causal effects on welfare."]},{"source_id":"SRC-989a4ab71d7e1333","start_unit":26,"end_unit":29,"fact_summary":"CONEVAL reported 2023 dissemination of 12 products, 139 media interviews, 11,687 media citations, 1,650,929 website visits, and survey results showing 98.7% positive perceptions of its contribution and 99.2% satisfaction with its analysis and recommendations; it also noted that 2024 indicator values were not yet available.","question_ids":["5B.7","6B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8"],"polarity":"favorable","period_fit":"The reported dissemination and perception results are for 2023; the unavailable 2024 values are explicitly outside the completed period.","ruler_attribution":"These are CONEVAL institutional results and do not establish personal presidential support or compliance.","limitations":["The perception survey covered 60 social-policy decision-makers and is not a population welfare measure.","High satisfaction does not demonstrate that policies achieved intended outcomes."]},{"source_id":"SRC-66941160fdec1f33","start_unit":4,"end_unit":6,"fact_summary":"The BTI report states that AMLO expanded the National Guard and military responsibilities, while cartel control and homicide remained substantial; it also reports that centralization and replacement of Seguro Popular with INSABI and then IMSS-Bienestar coincided with a 20% increase in the share lacking health-service access, medication shortages, austerity-related capacity loss, and expanded direct transfers with clientelist effects.","question_ids":["3B.2","3B.5","3B.6","3B.10","4B.4","5B.6","5B.10","6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.7","6B.9","6B.10","8B.2","8B.3","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The report is a later assessment covering AMLO's administration and uses 2022-2024 indicators; some details postdate 2023 and require caution for the target year.","ruler_attribution":"The report directly attributes the National Guard, health-system restructuring, austerity and transfer policies to AMLO's administration.","limitations":["The report page is labeled BTI 2026 despite the supplied title identifying it as BTI 2024.","Some statistics and institutional developments concern 2024 or later and are not contemporaneous evidence for 2023."]},{"source_id":"SRC-66941160fdec1f33","start_unit":7,"end_unit":10,"fact_summary":"BTI reports favorable and adverse economic evidence: poverty and wages improved and macroeconomic policy remained orthodox, but growth averaged about 1% under AMLO, 2023 FDI was below 2013, contracts were often directly awarded without tenders, environmental and Indigenous consultation was weak, R&D investment was cut, and decision-making was centralized with limited evidence-based evaluation and adaptation.","question_ids":["4B.3","4B.6","4B.7","5B.1","5B.2","5B.3","5B.4","5B.5","5B.6","5B.7","5B.8","5B.9","5B.10","6B.3","6B.5","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10","7B.7","7B.9","8B.1","8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.5","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The report evaluates AMLO's tenure and includes 2023 economic and institutional evidence, but also later comparative data.","ruler_attribution":"The report attributes the described policies and centralization to AMLO's government.","limitations":["The report is a retrospective country assessment and combines outcomes from multiple years.","Some causal explanations are expert judgments rather than direct administrative records."]},{"source_id":"SRC-66941160fdec1f33","start_unit":11,"end_unit":11,"fact_summary":"BTI reports that the AMLO government created commissions for historical crimes and Ayotzinapa but at points blocked access to army information, weakened or failed to protect victims' organizations, changed the methodology for counting disappearances, and did not effectively investigate more than 100,000 missing persons; it also notes public commitments to investigation and some institutional cooperation.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.4","3B.10","4B.4","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.10","8B.5","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The report assesses AMLO's administration and continuing disappearance-investigation policy, with some events spanning the full presidential term.","ruler_attribution":"BTI attributes the conduct to the AMLO government but does not prove personal presidential orders for each blockage or methodological change.","limitations":["The claims summarize a secondary assessment and include allegations about institutional motives.","The exact timing and scope of each interruption are not fully specified in the supplied unit."]},{"source_id":"SRC-d97a061e10c2ae4b","start_unit":3,"end_unit":14,"fact_summary":"BTI 2024 reports that AMLO expanded military involvement in security and economic activities despite campaign promises to reduce it; cartel influence, high homicide levels and impunity persisted; Plan B weakened electoral oversight; the president attacked journalists and autonomous organizations; and the Supreme Court's independence was pressured, although courts later invalidated parts of Plan B and the National Guard transfer.","question_ids":["3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.8","3B.10","4B.2","4B.3","4B.4","4B.6","4B.8","4B.9","4B.10","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.8","7B.10","8B.1","8B.2","8B.5","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The report covers February 2021-January 2023, with some events and judicial decisions occurring in early 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The report directly attributes the electoral, military, media and institutional policies to AMLO and his administration.","limitations":["The coverage ends in January 2023 and cannot establish the full-year 2023 outcome.","The report is an analytical assessment and includes forecasts and concerns about future effects."]},{"source_id":"SRC-d97a061e10c2ae4b","start_unit":24,"end_unit":28,"fact_summary":"BTI reports that AMLO expanded direct cash transfers and raised the minimum wage, but health coverage losses followed the abolition of Seguro Popular and creation of INSABI, cash programs were vulnerable to patronage, gender and Indigenous inequalities persisted, economic growth was weak, environmental policy favored fossil fuels and major projects harmed ecosystems, and R&D funding was cut.","question_ids":["5B.1","5B.6","5B.8","5B.10","6B.1","6B.2","6B.3","6B.4","6B.7","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10","8B.2","8B.3","8B.4","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The report covers policy and outcomes through January 2023, with indicators mainly from 2020-2022.","ruler_attribution":"BTI attributes the reforms, transfers, energy and research choices to AMLO's government.","limitations":["The report predates most of 2023 and therefore cannot capture subsequent implementation or correction.","Several welfare and environmental outcomes reflect inherited and pandemic conditions as well as AMLO-era choices."]},{"source_id":"SRC-f94bb5fa653e2226","start_unit":32,"end_unit":33,"fact_summary":"The 2023 CCC Index ranked Mexico 12th of 15 countries with a score of 3.87, down from 4.05 in 2022 and declining for the fourth consecutive year; it reported adverse conditions for journalists and civil society, AMLO's criticism of journalists and independent agencies, allegations of Pegasus surveillance, an INAI quorum crisis after his vetoes, and institutional shortcomings that hindered corruption-case resolution, while noting a 2023 anti-corruption budget increase and a Segalmex investigation.","question_ids":["4B.3","4B.4","4B.6","4B.9","5B.5","5B.7","7B.1","7B.2","7B.6","7B.7","7B.9","7B.10","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"adverse","period_fit":"The index was published in June 2023 and assesses the anti-corruption environment using current public and expert data.","ruler_attribution":"The report directly attributes criticism of journalists and agencies, commissioner vetoes and proposed institutional changes to AMLO.","limitations":["The index is a composite assessment based on 14 variables, public data and expert surveys; it is not a record of individual legal findings.","The report notes methodological subjectivity, overlap and incomplete coverage."]},{"source_id":"SRC-34635abd966dfd45","start_unit":12,"end_unit":16,"fact_summary":"The chapter argues that AMLO used populist polarization, daily attacks on journalists, civil society, scholars, scientists, lawyers, judges and feminists, reduced public research and civil-society funding, weakened state capacity through austerity, and produced chronic health and medicine shortages after replacing Seguro Popular with INSABI; it also notes expanded cash transfers and minimum-wage increases.","question_ids":["3B.3","3B.8","3B.9","3B.10","4B.3","4B.6","4B.9","4B.10","5B.6","5B.7","5B.10","6B.1","6B.2","6B.4","6B.8","6B.9","6B.10","7B.1","7B.8","7B.10","8B.2","8B.4","8B.6","8B.7","8B.8","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The chapter discusses AMLO's presidency and cites evidence available through early 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The author directly attributes the described rhetoric, funding, institutional and health policies to López Obrador.","limitations":["This is a scholarly interpretive chapter, not a comprehensive administrative dataset.","Some conclusions rely on cited secondary reporting and do not establish every causal link."]},{"source_id":"SRC-34635abd966dfd45","start_unit":17,"end_unit":23,"fact_summary":"The chapter reports that AMLO attacked and sought to weaken the INE, proposed electoral changes that would politicize its counselors, and advanced Plan B to shrink the institute; mass demonstrations and constitutional litigation followed, and the Supreme Court suspended and later invalidated Plan B portions for defective legislative procedure, despite continued governmental attacks.","question_ids":["4B.1","4B.2","4B.3","4B.4","4B.8","4B.9","4B.10","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The chapter covers the electoral conflict through the Supreme Court's May-June 2023 decisions.","ruler_attribution":"The chapter directly attributes the proposals, attacks and legislative strategy to AMLO and Morena.","limitations":["The source emphasizes constitutional and institutional dynamics rather than verified effects on electoral outcomes.","It records both adverse executive conduct and corrective action by civil society and courts."]},{"source_id":"SRC-34635abd966dfd45","start_unit":24,"end_unit":30,"fact_summary":"The chapter reports that AMLO created and militarized the National Guard, expanded military control over public security, ports, customs and infrastructure, and enacted rules with weak safeguards for detention, use of force and public information; in April 2023 the Supreme Court invalidated the transfer of the National Guard to military control, ordering civilian control from January 2024, while the Inter-American Court rejected automatic preventive detention and arraigo.","question_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.5","3B.8","3B.10","4B.4","4B.9","7B.6","7B.7","8B.2","8B.5","8B.8","8B.9","8B.10"],"polarity":"mixed","period_fit":"The chapter includes policies during AMLO's term and judicial decisions in April 2023.","ruler_attribution":"The chapter directly attributes the National Guard, military-control and decree policies to AMLO; judicial corrections are attributed to the Supreme Court and Inter-American Court.","limitations":["The chapter is doctrinal and analytical; it does not provide complete operational data on military conduct.","Some statutory defects are legal interpretations rather than final findings on every individual incident."]}],"documents_with_no_material_fact":[],"batch_limitations":["The supplied documents vary substantially in period: some assess 2023 directly, while others cover earlier years or include post-2023 retrospective evidence.","Facts are attributed to López Obrador only where the source expressly links him or his administration to the action; institutional or collective Mexican-state findings are qualified accordingly.","No source supplied material evidence for most nuclear command, custody, proliferation-control, AI, biological-risk, or conventional-war questions beyond the TPNW proceedings; those questions are omitted from individual fact mappings where unsupported."]}
